summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted for bilateral groin pain, which he had been experiencing for one day and which initially improved after his long-standing indwelling Foley catheter was changed in the emergency department. The pain returned with lesser intensity, but there were no signs of active infection such as fever or leukocytosis. Urinalysis showed pyuria and bacteriuria, but repeat testing revealed improvement and the urine culture showed no growth, supporting the conclusion that the findings represented colonization rather than infection. The groin pain and hematuria were attributed to catheter-related trauma. His daughter reported a mechanical fall five days prior with head impact; a non-contrast head CT showed no acute intracranial process. Due to generalized weakness and safety concerns, physical therapy recommended rehabilitation, which the patient accepted after initial hesitation. He was discharged to an extended care facility for physical therapy and close monitoring, with instructions to change his Foley catheter every 4 to 6 weeks and follow up with urology.
